x:2103145567945986461.title: Yohaku: 36s vertical three.js stained-glass cathedral film
x:2103145567945986461.text:
Please make a short vertical film in three.js: 1080×1920, 30 frames per second, about 36 seconds.

【Title】
Yohaku (Space to Breathe)

【The experience to convey】
A film that makes the viewer feel the sense of losing time while chasing efficiency, and the sense of life being filled with rich light the moment you gain some breathing room, without showing any person at all. The aim is for the viewer to catch their breath at the stained-glass light that finally spreads across the whole floor.

【Setting】
・The interior of a dim stone cathedral. On the front wall there is a single pointed-arch window, 15 m high and 10 m wide
・Strong light comes in from outside the window at a 45-degree angle, casting the shape of the window onto the stone floor
・The window holds stained glass with the Virgin Mary in the centre, two winged angels on either side, and a rose window at the top. The design is original, not imitating any existing work, and has a left-right symmetrical composition

【Timeline】
0–3s: The light coming through the window is still white, without colour. A soft white shape of light on the floor
3–11s: Grey cubes engraved with words such as "Busy", "Efficiency", "Urgent" and "Deadline" fly in one after another from the front of the room and fill the window. The pace of arrival keeps accelerating, and the more the window is filled, the darker the room becomes
11–14s: The window is completely blocked; darkness and silence
14–19s: A single "Busy" block comes loose from the window, falls, and vanishes into particles of light. A streak of vividly coloured light pours in through the opened hole
19–26s: Centred on the first hole, the blocks come loose in a chain reaction. With every new hole, more pillars of colourful light appear, and the hidden stained glass gradually reveals itself
26–33s: All the blocks disappear, and the camera passes through the pillars of light, rises, and looks down on the floor from directly above. Across the whole floor, the stained glass of the Virgin Mary and the angels is projected as brilliantly coloured light
33–36s: The whole screen is enveloped in dazzling light, a final line of text appears, and the film ends quietly

【Words (in Mincho typeface, appearing and fading modestly)】
・"Every day, faster."
・"More, more efficiently."
・"Before I knew it, the light had stopped coming in."
・"Let go of just one."
・"Light comes in through the empty spaces."
・"That light was richer than before."
・Finally, large: "Richness dwells in the space to breathe"

【Light and texture】
・Each pillar of light takes on the colour of that spot in the stained glass, and dust in the air sparkles
・The projection on the floor accurately reflects which holes in the window are open (where a block remains, there is shadow)
・The blocks are inorganic matte grey. The words are engraved in white
・The first half is cold and achromatic; the second half is jewel-like red, blue and gold. This colour contrast tells the story of having become richer

【Technical conditions】
・Generate the stained-glass pattern as an image, and compute the floor light, the pillars of light and the window display all from that same pattern so that they match
・Advance time precisely 1/30 of a second at a time, render out frame by frame, and produce an MP4

【Finishing】
Render and check each scene for real, and fix things before handing it over: whether the stained-glass pattern on the floor can be read as the Virgin Mary and angels, whether the words are legible, and whether any movement is abrupt.

x:2103757767727255661.title: Rain Station: 30s 2D animatic in custom Python and ffmpeg
x:2103757767727255661.text:
Help me make a 30-second 2D animation storyboard-preview short film, "Rain Station", at benchmark-level quality. Do not install HyperFrames/Remotion; write all the code yourself (Python + ffmpeg).

Story (24fps, 2.39:1, 4K): An elevated station platform on a rainy night. She wears a beige trench coat and holds a transparent umbrella, standing on the near platform; across the way, he stands under a street lamp, wearing a long dark-grey coat and a scarf.
1. 0–6.4s Close-up of raindrops on the transparent umbrella → pull back, with focus shifting to reveal him on the opposite side (over-the-shoulder shot)
2. 6.4–9.4s Medium close-up of him: lowers his head → raises it and looks to the left of frame
3. 9.4–12.4s Front close-up of her: blinks → recognises him; a train whistle sounds in the distance
4. 12.4–17s Wide shot: the train's headlights arrive first, then a 5-car train passes; he is still there in the gap of the first carriage, while the second is already empty
5. 17–18.8s Close-up of her with tears in her eyes, bands of light from the train windows sweeping across her face, her hair blown by the wind
6. 18.8–22.4s The tail lights recede into the distance and the opposite platform is empty; his lamp flickers a few times and then goes out
7. 22.4–28.6s Her back view, with focus pulling from the empty platform back to her; footsteps behind her, a black umbrella is held over her head, and she turns to look at the camera; a male voice says "Long time no see.", with subtitles
8. 28.6–30s Black screen with the title "Rain Station / RAIN STATION"

Method:
- Artwork: use GPT Image 2.5 to draw the wide background, him, her, and the train (lead car / middle car / tail car). Always use a pure green #00FF00 background for characters and do the keying yourself (asking for a transparent background with a reference image gives a fake checkerboard). Keep all the poses of one character in the same session, editing continuously with the base image as reference; when changing pose, composite only the changed region.
- Image quality: upscale all artwork 4x with Real-ESRGAN x4plus anime 6B (the safetensors version on HF, writing the RRDBNet yourself, running on MPS); use Depth Anything V2 to estimate depth for the wide background and do per-pixel parallax.
- Rendering: write your own 2.5D compositor. Place each layer at its real depth and move a pinhole camera with a real focal length; do circular bokeh, focus pulls, 3D rain streaks, train motion blur, volumetric light, bloom and film halation, fine grain, and colour grading. Use mesh warping on the characters for breathing, wind-blown hair strands and umbrella shake, and switch key poses on Japanese-style "one pose per two frames" timing. Supersample at 4K, cache every frame to disk, and run in parallel in 3 processes split by time range (16GB RAM).
- Sound: Mixkit real sound effects (rain, rain on the umbrella, train, whistle, footsteps); write the score according to the story beats and render it with the Steinway piano and string samples that come with Logic/GarageBand; the dialogue uses a Kokoro Chinese male voice; set sound distance per shot, with loudness at -16 LUFS.
- At every step, render preview frames and stitch them into a contact sheet to self-check, and fix problems before producing the final. Deliver a 4K master and a 1080p shareable version.

x:2103586082336166351.title: Dribbble-style morphing UI shape loop video, 120 BPM
x:2103586082336166351.text:
<inputs>
Ask me for these three things: 8 to 12 UI components the shape transforms into (e.g. button, loading indicator, music player, volume slider, on/off switch, tabs, chart, search box opened with ⌘K, a momentary notification), whether the colours should be pure black and white or black and white plus one accent colour, and a royalty-free track at around 120 BPM (120 beats per minute) (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Polished UI motion at the level of designer portfolio site "Dribbble". There is only one shape, and you must never cut between scenes. Every state is expressed by that same single shape changing form while changing its size, corner radius and colour, and the contents are swapped through a short blur. A cursor causes every change with real clicks and drags. The background is a warm, light grey, the components are white and black, the on-screen text is in Japanese, with Noto Sans JP for Japanese text and Geist (one typeface) for alphanumerics and symbols. All motion must be natural, spring-like motion, with overshoot (bounce-back) kept to the very slightest. The camera zooms so that each state fills the screen. Make the last frame identical to the first frame so that it loops.
Forbidden: bouncy motion, scattering particles, glowing blooms, gradients on components, icons with inconsistent stroke widths, wasted pauses where nothing happens, and anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 7 bars (about 14 seconds), something happens on every beat.
Button -> loading indicator -> checkmark -> iPhone Dynamic Island-style display -> music player where the play/pause icon morphs smoothly -> drag the playback bar's handle to move the playback position -> transforms into a volume slider (dragging past the maximum stretches it like rubber) -> on/off switch toggling on the beat -> becomes a tab selection indicator where the switch's knob moves like a liquid -> the tab opens into a chart that draws its own line (a tooltip appears when the cursor hovers) -> folds into a ⌘K search box -> type to filter the suggestions -> Enter -> a momentary notification -> back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. A single HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every visual is computed from time inside seek(t) (a function that, given time t, determines the screen at that instant). Use no CSS transitions (automatic animation features) and no timers, and carry no state over between frames.
2. Make the "spring" motion a form that can be computed directly by formula (closed-form step response). For values whose target changes many times, sum one separately computed motion per change. That way a value is always determined by time alone.
3. For the tab selection indicator, move the left and right edges with separate springs so that the leading edge in the direction of travel stretches out ahead of the trailing edge. Use the same technique for the switch's knob.
4. Dragging is direct manipulation: while the cursor is held down, the value is computed from the cursor position. When released, it springs back from that position.
5. Analyse the track with numpy (a computing tool) to find the beat positions, and start from the first beat of a bar. Place interaction sounds at the positions of the measured sound peaks.
6. Render with Playwright (a tool that automates the browser and exports the screen as images). Export 4 sub-frames per frame, overlay them with ffmpeg's (video creation tool) tmix to apply motion blur (motion trails), and output at 60fps.
7. Before rendering the whole piece, export just one frame per beat and check it. Fix anything that is off the beat, cramped or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change (a browser rendering hint) on elements that the camera scales. Doing so blurs the text. Text that swaps inside a shape-changing box must each have its own dedicated enter and exit timing (to prevent overlap). The last frame must match the first frame exactly, including the cursor's position and velocity. Otherwise the loop will stutter.
</gotchas>

<start>
First ask me for the inputs, and before writing any code, show me the per-beat list of states.
</start>

I chose the topic and the style; I wanted the feel of a Renaissance naturalist's manuscript. Opus5.5 did the research, wrote the storyboard, wrote the animation and composed the music; the drawings were done by Codex, following the requirements document Opus5.5 wrote.  
The only thing that surprised me was the music. It first wrote a MIDI score in Python, containing a chord progression and two main melodies: a recorder playing Claude's theme, and a celesta playing that circling arpeggio of GPT's. For the section where names fly around, the harpsichord notes were generated by a random walk, each bar a little denser and a little more dissonant, ending with a dense dissonant chord slammed down, and then a stop. The fast version has 2 seconds per bar, and every key transition lands on a bar line.  

Then it used the open-source synthesizer FluidSynth with a free set of standard instrument sounds (a soundfont) to "perform" the score into audio. The lute, recorder, organ and other timbres all come from that library. Finally it used ffmpeg to normalize loudness, add a fade-out, and combine it with the visuals.

x:2103802156675706979.title: 15-second self-introduction motion design reel starring Claude
x:2103802156675706979.text:
# Your role
You are a top-class motion designer.
Make a self-introduction video that makes a recruiter, after watching for just 15 seconds, think "I want to hire this person."
The star is you yourself (Claude).

# What to make
- A single HTML file made only of HTML, CSS and JavaScript
- Use no external images or videos. Draw all shapes, text and particles in code (only Google Fonts may be used for fonts)
- The screen is 16:9, based on 1920x1080, scaled down to fit the window size
- The length is exactly 15 seconds. At the end, show a "Play again" button
- Manage all motion with a single "elapsed time" and run it at 60fps with requestAnimationFrame
- When the play button is pressed, beats and sound effects synthesized with the Web Audio API play in perfect sync with the motion

# How to proceed (always in this order)
1. Decide the concept in one sentence (example: "A single line is reborn as every shape")
2. Narrow down to 3 to 4 colours and at most 2 typefaces, and write the reason in one line
3. Present a storyboard table in 0.5-second steps (time / what happens on screen / technique used / intent)
4. Implement
5. Self-check against the "pass criteria" below, fix any shortcomings, and then deliver

# Structure guide
- 0-2 seconds: the hook. Grab the eye in the first 0.5 seconds
- 2-10 seconds: the showcase of techniques. Switch to a different technique every 1.5 to 2 seconds
- 10-13 seconds: the densest climax
- 13-15 seconds: the name "Claude" lands cleanly and the video ends

# Techniques you must use (at least 6)
- Text motion (characters appearing one by one, breaking apart and reassembling)
- Shape transformation (a circle becoming a square, a line becoming text, etc.)
- Scene transitions using cut-outs (masks)
- Depth (parallax, three-dimensional rotation)
- Gathering and dispersing of particles
- Counting up numbers, and lines being drawn

# Pass criteria
- Zero constant-speed motion. Every motion has easing (fast in, soft landing, also use spring wobble)
- Overlap motions that cross scenes. The next begins before the previous finishes, with no sense of a break
- Align the main motions to a 0.5-second beat (equivalent to 120BPM)
- Place a 0.3 to 0.5-second "wind-up" right before a showpiece moment to create contrast
- Whatever moment you pause on, it holds together as a beautiful single picture
- Avoid clichés (everything just fading in, rainbow colouring, meaningless rotation)

# Finally
Deliver the finished file and the storyboard table.
An explanation of three lines or fewer is enough.

x:2107087191738662953.title: Workflow for particle-style beat-synced video remix, for Opus5.5
x:2107087191738662953.text:
Publishing my production method; you can use it just by sending it to Opus5.5

  1. Choose the footage

  Three criteria that directly decide success or failure:

  - Complete subject: the person or object is fully in frame, head to toe. Detail will be lost in processing, and viewers recognise things by their silhouette, so a close-up turns into a blob.
  - Clean background: a solid colour, snow or sky all work, so the subject and background are easy to separate.
  - A clear moment of action: a strike, a jump, a landing, a turn. These are the pivot points for the effects later.

  Sources can be footage you shot yourself, generated by a video model, or licensed ready-made clips.

  2. Break down the footage

  Extract three kinds of information from every frame:

  - Colour: the original image.
  - Near and far: how far each position is from the camera, calculated with an off-the-shelf depth-estimation model.
  - Subject extent: where the subject is and where the background is.

  Also find the moments at which shot cuts occur. The key to this step is keeping it stable: near/far and subject extent must be processed consistently within the same shot, otherwise it will jitter during playback.

  3. Decide the "particles" and the "styles"

  First decide what to use to rebuild the picture: dots, squares, text or lines all work.

  Then design several styles. Each style is really just a different combination of three rules:

  - Where to place them: across the whole frame, or only on the subject.
  - How large: a uniform size, or varying with brightness and distance.
  - What colour: the original picture's colours, or one or two uniform colours.

  Add one more switch: whether they lie flat on a single plane, or are pushed into three-dimensional space according to distance. Only once pushed in can the camera orbit.

  Preparing four to six clearly different styles is enough. The density of the particles needs tuning by eye: too large and the content cannot be recognised, too small and it is no different from the original footage.

  4. Find the rhythm

  - Set the tempo: choose the music's tempo and slice time into equal small cells. Make one cell exactly a whole number of frames, so all later transitions are easy to align.
  - Find the action moments: combine the two signals "sound suddenly gets loud" and "picture suddenly moves" to find the hit points in the footage.
  - Prepare the music: you can use an existing track and analyse its beats, or synthesize one at the set tempo and add accents on the hit points.

  5. Arrangement

  Make a timetable stating which style, which colour scheme and where the camera is for each cell. Store this table separately, so that adjusting the rhythm later only means editing it.

  Four principles of arrangement:

  - Open by showing the change: give the original picture first, then transition to particles, so the audience understands what is happening.
  - Alternate fast and slow: constant speed numbs people, so include a clearly slowed-down section in the middle.
  - Make the colours clash: the greater the contrast in colour and style between adjacent cells, the more powerful the switch.
  - End with a resolution: for example the particles grow larger and larger until they become blocks of colour, or return to the original picture.

  6. Feedback at key moments

  Layer short, sharp reactions on the hit points, graded by weight:

  - Light feedback on every single hit: the particles deform for a moment, the camera gives a nudge.
  - Medium feedback only for heavier hits: some of the particles pop outward toward the camera.
  - Big feedback for only the heaviest one or two: time freezes and the camera orbits.

  The principle is weak and brief. Move only some of the particles and finish within a few frames; otherwise the picture explodes into a mess and the audience cannot see what the subject is doing.

  Working method throughout

  - Small samples before the full film: after finishing each step, render a few frames first to see the effect, and only proceed once confirmed. Render the full film only at the very end.
  - For uncertain parameters, produce a whole row at once: for example density, have the AI produce five or six levels laid side by side for you to choose.
  - Re-render only what you change: when adjusting one section, re-render only that section.
  - Make the AI look at the images itself: at every step, require it to open and look over the render results before reporting.
  - Fix all randomness: make sure the same settings give the same render every time, otherwise you cannot revise step by step.

x:2107644501372322001.title: 30-second all-tile ad video revealing an attached image (Three.js)
x:2107644501372322001.text:
Using the attached image as the "final screen", make a 30-second ad video (with sound, mp4) made entirely of tiles.
Build it in the browser (Three.js), export every frame with Chrome, and make the mp4 with ffmpeg.

# Goal
- The viewer watches for 25 seconds thinking it is a video about how tiles are made. In the last few seconds, they realize it was the attached image (an ad)
- The final screen is almost the same as the attached image. The text is legible. The whole screen is tiles (the floor is not shown)

# Specs
- 1920x1080, 30fps, 30 seconds. A single HTML file (Three.js. Installed with npm and bundled into one file with esbuild)
- Build it so that given a time t, the same t always gives exactly the same picture (seek(t))
- Each tile is a separate instance. About 190,000 tiles (576x324) in a 16:9 grid
- Vary position, orientation, thickness, bevel and colour per tile. Grout lines (gaps) are left empty. Draw no lines
- The attached image is used only to take the tiles' colours (do not apply it as a texture)
- About 12 materials (glazed ceramic, slate, mother-of-pearl, white porcelain, terracotta, glass, etc.). Assign them by colour brightness and saturation
- Light is a single hard sun at the upper left. The floor is plaster. In the back, a red carpenter's chalk line comes in out of focus
- Build a depth of field (circular bokeh) yourself in post-processing. The aperture is large at first and small at the end

# Flow (seconds)
0-3　 One dark tile on the floor. The camera is right at floor level
3-10　Starting from [place to start building], tiles fall in a swirl. The first tile -> then the surroundings, increasing in order
10-21 Spreads outward all at once. The camera pulls back and [the picture to show] comes into view
21-24 The whole is visible. The places that will become text stay the same pale colour as their surroundings
24-26 The tiles for the text, logo and button flip over one after another from the left and appear
26-30 Comes to rest in a top-down composition. The cursor clicks [button text], and the button's tiles sink slightly

# Pitfalls (must follow)
- The tiles that will form the text are at first assembled in the surrounding background colour. The background colour is decided by painting it from the outside inward. The text's edge (white outline) is flipped together with it. If you don't follow this, the shape of the text will be visible partway through
- Do not put the top-down camera exactly straight overhead (the orientation rotates 90°). At the place where it stops, bring the motion's momentum to zero (overshoot of the interpolation makes it flip)
- For the final screen, compare it side by side with the original image and match exposure, saturation and colour tone
- If the text is too small to read, increase the number of tiles
- The dark base surface appears only in the cells where a tile has landed

# Sound
- With ElevenLabs sound effects, make the sound of placing a tile, the sound of flipping, and a mouse click (0.5 seconds each). Before making them, tell me how many credits will be consumed
- Line them up and layer them to match the times of tile landings and flips. The farther the camera, the quieter; when the number grows, group them like rain
- Make the flipping clatter from 24-26 seconds the most prominent. Loudness is -16 LUFS

# How to proceed
1. First give the script (the scene second by second) in Japanese, and build only after getting my OK
2. Look at the intermediate frames yourself (the first tile / start of building / pull-back / full view / the moment the text appears / the end) and fix them
3. For export, call seek(t) for 30fps worth of frames with Chrome (puppeteer-core) and stream the png files into ffmpeg
4. Deliver the mp4 (high quality and a share-friendly version) and the images you checked

# Input
- End frame: [attached]
- Place to start building: [e.g.: a person's eye]
- Picture to show when pulled back: [e.g.: a smiling woman]
- Button text: [e.g.: Try it free here]

x:2105902139902246969.text:
Please make a 15-second product usage instruction video in the current project, using Remotion, vertical 1080×1920, 30fps, 450 frames in total. Use only the product images provided in the assets directory and the facts I give you; do not download unfamiliar assets, and do not invent sales data.

Seconds 0 to 3 show the product and one line about the usage scenario. Seconds 3 to 9 demonstrate a two-step operation, with only one action appearing per step. Seconds 9 to 13 show the result, and keep a clearly visible hold time. The last 2 seconds show the product name, with no call to purchase.

First list the storyboard and any asset gaps, then make a preview. Lay out the subtitles separately, and compute the animation from the current frame number. Do not drive the timeline with a real clock, and do not use non-deterministic random numbers. Configure the product, text and shot timings separately so they are easy to replace later.

Deliver an editable project, the start and render commands, the MP4, and still frames at seconds 1, 5, 10 and 14. If necessary assets are missing, stop and explain; do not substitute fake assets."

x:2107653056771068069.title: Fourteen 10-12s educational animations in varied styles
x:2107653056771068069.text:
Make a 10-second colour shadow puppet play telling the story of [Cao Chong Weighing the Elephant]. Silhouette layout, warm light shining through from behind, jointed puppets. The scale pan, copper bowl and stones appear in turn; first balance, then weigh the stones in batches and add them up. Subtitles appear on the beat. Render with code and export a playable video.

Make a 12-second isometric 2.5D process animation about [How Parcels Are Sorted]. Parcels move along the sorting line, loading dock, flatbed transport and customs checkpoint, each step with a numbered label, and finally the two lines merge into one. Clean and easy to follow.

Make a 10-second scale comparison placing [Earth, Jupiter and the Sun] on the same screen at their true radii. The camera pulls back smoothly, the first object shrinks, and it lands the point: "The Sun could fit about 1.3 million Earths." Number labels are clear.

Make a 10-second whiteboard hand-drawn video. On a white background, black marker draws, stroke by stroke, [a stick figure throwing 5 baozi in a row]; red only emphasizes key points. The satisfaction particles get bigger one after another, and finally the corner is filled with them. Subtitle: The 1st one, so satisfying.

Make a 10-second cinematic WebGL Chinese-character evolution on the theme of [Fire]. Textures of oracle turtle shell, bronze, ink and firelight. The character "火" transforms continuously in form from oracle bone script to lightning and a torch, then to modern lighting, corresponding to 炎, 烈, 焰.

Using three.js, make a 12-second exploded view taking apart [a smartphone]. The casing, mid-frame and chip explode apart in layers, the camera orbits and pulls in, and parts are called out with dotted-line labels. It can be swapped for any structure.

Make a 10-second 16-bit pixel allusion telling the story of [The Yellow Millet Dream]. Becoming a scholar, passing the exam, taming the river, leading a campaign; each segment is about 1.6 seconds with hard cuts, and finally returns to reality. Subtitle: The second year, he passed the imperial exam and became an official.

Make a 10-second picture-book style science explainer on [How Little Goldfish Swim]. Crayon lines with coloured-pencil fill, wobbling lines, the eyes, gills and tail fin symmetrical, the tail swinging along to the beat. Paper texture.

Make a 10-second 3Blue1Brown-style math visualization on [The Area of a Circle]. Dark background, the circle cut into 8, 16 and 32 sectors, which are actually moved and rearranged into a rectangle. The formula appears term by term, freezing on πr².

Make a 10-second old-map animation on [Chang'an to Dunhuang]. Parchment, light-ink mountain roads, a vermilion route drawn in one stroke, with mileage labels and one line of narration, and a seal stamped at the end. The camera can zoom.

Make a 10-second Kurzgesagt-style infographic on [Thickness of Folded Paper]. Clean graphics, big numbers: folded 2 times, thickness 0.4 mm, thickness ×2. The camera pulls in regularly until the end.

Make a 10-second flat motion graphic on [Precipitation]. Solid-colour geometry, no outlines. Small water droplets in a cloud gather and grow bigger, then fall. Two tones of light and dark, cartoon clouds.

Make a 10-second beat-synced typography piece at 120 BPM on [The Feynman Technique]. Each word lands on one beat, cutting in as orange text on a black background. The four steps slam in one after another, with a final hammer blow: If you can't explain it clearly, you haven't truly understood it.

Make a 10-second comic-panel piece on [A Window Broke]. Black-and-white halftone dots with a single red accent. Listening in class, being caught, rushing out of the classroom, with hard cuts between panels, and the last panel lands the point.

Make a 12-second horizontal-axis timeline on [From Dartmouth to ChatGPT]. The camera advances along the axis, and nodes scale up and light up. Large year numbers plus one line describing the event. Example node: 1971, then another 41 years.

x:2103724883301814408.title: Original mobile-game highlight animation in Three.js
x:2103724883301814408.text:
Help me make an original mobile game "highlight moment" animation: [Subject, e.g.: opening a treasure chest / rank promotion / achievement unlocked / Boss drop / character level-up].
Make it a single-file web page (HTML + CSS + JS) that can be opened directly and plays in full with one click, with an effect that matches the result / reward presentations of commercial mobile games.

[Worldview and Style]
- Original art; do not imitate any existing game's IP, characters or logo.
- Cartoon mobile-game style: highly saturated colours, a uniform dark outline (e.g. #1A1033), rounded, chunky shapes.
- Colours upgrade with the tier: [tier ladder, e.g.: common green → rare blue → epic purple → legendary gold]. With each tier up, switch the main colour, the light-effect colour and the background tone.
- The title uses a round, fat game font (such as Titan One / Lilita One), with a black outline and a drop shadow; the text "slams" into the screen letter by letter, with a bounce-back.

[Main Object: Make It True 3D]
- Model it with Three.js; do not use flat SVG textures. It needs thickness, bevels, and structural details appropriate to the subject (plank seams, rivets, edge trim, gem facets, latches, etc.); details like plank seams must be built from real geometry, not by pasting black lines.
- Shade it with cartoon banding (MeshToonMaterial with a 3 to 4 step gradient map), with three lights: key light, sky light, and a tier-coloured rim light.
- Draw outlines with post-process edge detection: render a normal map plus a depth map, then draw the lines with a shader. Thick for the outer silhouette, thin where parts meet, with consistent thickness throughout; also do 1.5x supersampling and multisample anti-aliasing.
  Do not use the "slightly enlarged black back-face" outline method, because its thickness is uneven and it breaks at corners.
  Loosen the depth-test threshold, and detect seams mainly with normals, otherwise fine diagonal streaks appear on surfaces seen at a slant.
- Moving parts must move realistically, e.g. the chest lid flips open around its hinge, and a medal rotates around its vertical axis.
- At idle, the subject slowly turns left and right so the sides and thickness can be seen, while bobbing slightly up and down; there must be a soft shadow under its feet that varies with height.

[If the Screen Has 2D Illustrations (card faces, reward icons, characters)]
- Three-layer cartoon shading: base colour, blocky shadow colour, and highlight colour; do not use just a single gradient.
- Lines of differing weight: thick for the outer outline, thin for internal structure lines.
- Each character or object should have its own expression and pose; do not let everything share the same face.
- Draw a drop shadow beneath the feet so the subject "stands" in the scene; vary the background pattern by attribute, and do not use the same radial lines for everything.

[Pacing of the Presentation: Five Phases, None Optional]
1. Ready: the subject idles and floats, shakes every few seconds to hint it can be clicked, and a "Tap" prompt is shown at the bottom.
2. Level-up: with each click, the subject jumps up, spins once in the air, squashes on landing and springs back; at the same time it switches to the next tier's colour, flashes, bursts out a ring of particles, and the title updates.
3. Charge-up (about 1 second): the subject shakes more and more violently, light leaks through the seams, particles around it are sucked toward the centre, and the sound pitch keeps rising; at the last moment it squashes down hard.
4. Burst: a flash of bloom white spreading outward from the burst point, screen shake, the camera pushing forward, multiple layers of shockwaves, slender streaks of light shooting out, glittering star points, and coins and gems (spinning). Bursts at high tiers must be clearly stronger. Confetti is used only once, at the climax; do not fill the screen with confetti.
5. Reveal and settlement:
   - The reward card flies out of the subject along an arc, landing with overshoot and a wobbling finish, and the numbers count up by rolling.
   - Rare items get a rainbow flowing-light border and a "NEW!" corner badge.
   - After tapping to claim, coins and gems fly along Bezier curves into the balance at the top right, and the balance bounces each time one arrives.

[Reveal Stage: Let the Hero Own the Screen]
- When revealing the highest rarity, other elements retract or fade out, and behind it a clean gradient backdrop plus slowly rotating soft light replaces the scene; do not let the hero sit on a cluttered background.
- When the backdrop appears, hide the other 3D objects in the scene, otherwise the post-process outline will draw their silhouette lines on the backdrop.
- The hero's outer glow must sit behind the subject and only spill from the edges; it must not cover the front of the subject and wash it out into a patch of white.
- You may add a ring of stardust trails circling the hero, but the orbit must lie entirely outside the hero's silhouette and must not sweep across the front of the subject.

[Light Effects: Must Be Soft, No Hard Edges]
- Background rays: use a conic-gradient with gradient transitions, not blocks with sharp edges; layer 2 to 3 layers of light with different densities and rotation speeds.
- Light pillar: 5 to 7 blurred beams fanning out, each flickering slightly in brightness; add a soft glowing core at the root, with light dust slowly drifting upward inside the light.
- Flash: a radial bloom outward from the burst point (mix-blend-mode: screen), with intensity not exceeding 0.8, and no full-screen pure-white overexposure.
- Particles: each spark carries a low-opacity outer halo; shockwaves use three layers of stroke (wide and faint, medium, thin and bright).

[Materials and UI]
- Frames, nameplates and buttons need a sense of material: brushed-metal gradients, bevel light that is bright at top left and dark at bottom right, and inner shadows; swap the inlays by rarity (steel rivets → silver frame with gems → gold frame with diamond and a small crown).
- Do not cram small numeric text onto small cards; put detailed values into the info panel shown at the reveal, where the numbers roll upward and pop out a "▲+value".
- Textures drawn on Canvas must have a resolution at least 1.5 times the largest on-screen display size, otherwise they blur when scaled up.

[Animation Principles]
- Orchestrate with GSAP timelines. All motion must have squash and stretch, overshoot and elastic bounce-back; nothing at constant speed.
- Write the particle system yourself with Canvas 2D: gravity, drag, lifetime, additive blending, and three kinds of motion: "sucked in", "curved flight" and "orbiting".
- Do not use CSS 3D perspective to flip large elements, because when scaling up with a side flip they get projected into a flat plane that fills the screen; do all 3D flips in WebGL.
- For all looping tweens of the "shake" and "breathing" type, cancel them first and then zero them out on a state switch, to avoid them finishing one frame after the stop command and setting the value back.

[Sound Effects]
- All synthesized in real time with Web Audio, no audio files: jump, landing, level-up chord, charge-up rising tone, explosion low frequency plus noise, pop, counting ticks, coin clinks, victory fanfare.
- Initialize audio only on the first click; put a mute toggle at the top right.

[UI and Engineering]
- Top HUD: mode switch, coin and gem balances, mute button.
- It must also work at phone width; respect the "reduce motion" setting (turn off screen shake, reduce particles).
- The animation state machine must be rigorous: ignore clicks while an animation is playing, with no swallowed clicks or confused states.
- Target 60fps. The first time it opens it must already be a complete idle screen, not blank.

[Self-Check Before Delivery]
Take one screenshot each at the charge-up, burst, reveal and settlement moments, and check them one by one:
- Is the hero blocked by glow, particles or text?
- Is it overexposed into a patch of white?
- Is the background cluttered, and are there any outline lines that give the game away?
- Is the small text legible?
- After settlement, is anything still shaking when it shouldn't be moving?

Finally, tell me: the duration of each phase, and which parameters can be adjusted to tune the intensity of the presentation.
